eyebrow: Python for Data Science · Chapter 2, Lesson 10
subtitle: Answering "what would happen if..." by running the experiment thousands of times.

code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.random(3))
# [0.77395605 0.43887844 0.85859792]

# Same seed -> identical sequence every time
caption: 42 is the seed — it makes your analysis reproducible for a teammate, or for you next month.

code:
rng.integers(1, 7, size=10)              # dice, 1-6
rng.normal(loc=100, scale=15, size=5)    # bell curve
rng.uniform(10, 20, size=3)              # evenly 10-20
rng.exponential(scale=50, size=3)        # skewed data
caption: integers(1, 7) excludes the upper end, just like range(). loc/scale are the mean/std of normal().

code:
a = np.array(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"])
rng.choice(a, size=3, replace=False)
rng.choice(["heads", "tails"], size=5, p=[0.7, 0.3])
rng.permutation(5)   # shuffled copy of 0..4
caption: choice samples with replacement by default; replace=False avoids repeats; p weights the odds.

code:
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100000, 2)).sum(axis=1)
print((rolls == 7).mean())   # 0.16775
# exact answer: 6/36 = 0.1667
caption: Roll two dice 100,000 times, sum each row, then average the boolean rolls==7.

eyebrow: The same trick for a business question
code:
churned = rng.random(1000) < 0.15
print(churned.sum())
# seed 1 -> 143 customers churned out of 1,000
caption: A different seed gives a slightly different count — that's the natural variation to expect.

eyebrow: Why averages of samples behave predictably
code:
orders = rng.exponential(scale=50, size=100000)
means = rng.choice(orders, size=(2000, 50)).mean(axis=1)
print(means.std())                 # ~7.07
print(orders.std() / np.sqrt(50))  # ~7.02
caption: Sample means cluster tightly, and their spread matches theory — the seed of the central limit theorem.

eyebrow: The bootstrap: resampling to gauge uncertainty
code:
x = np.array([12, 15, 11, 18, 14, 22, 9, 16])
bm = rng.choice(x, size=(5000, len(x)), replace=True).mean(axis=1)
print(x.mean())                        # 14.625
print(np.percentile(bm, [2.5, 97.5]))  # [12. 17.375]
caption: The 2.5th-97.5th percentile range of resampled means is a rough 95% interval for the true mean.
